units.title: Getting started
units.blurb: What Avalonia is and how it differs from WPF and MAUI, a first project from a template, and AXAML markup.

lessons.title: What is Avalonia
lessons.sub: One C# and XAML UI for every system

cards.title: C# windows, everywhere
cards.body:
Avalonia is a framework for apps with windows, buttons and lists. Write it once in C# and XAML, and run it on Windows, macOS and Linux, plus iOS, Android and the browser.

It is open source under the MIT license.

cards.title: It draws itself
cards.body:
Usually a button in an app is an operating system button. Avalonia works differently: it draws every pixel itself with the Skia graphics library, like a game engine.

That is why an app looks the same everywhere, and supporting a new platform comes down to "learn to open a window and draw in it".

cards.q: Why does an Avalonia app look the same on Windows and macOS?
options: Avalonia draws every element itself with Skia instead of using system buttons
It copies the Windows style onto the Mac
cards.explain: Custom rendering is the core idea behind Avalonia.

cards.title: The neighbors
cards.body:
WPF: Microsoft's XAML framework, Windows only. Avalonia is similar in many ways, and WPF experience carries over.
WinForms: the old forms, Windows only.
.NET MAUI: also cross-platform, but builds the UI from each system's native controls.

cards.q: Match each framework to its key trait
Where can an Avalonia app run? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Plus iOS, Android and embedded Linux with no windowing system.

cards.q: You know WPF. What will feel familiar in Avalonia?
options: XAML, bindings, styles, MVVM: same ideas, different details
cards.explain: There are differences too: a different selector-based style system and different names for some properties. We will cover them along the way.

cards.title: The price of custom rendering
cards.body: The look is not fully native: a button on a Mac looks like an Avalonia button, not a macOS one. For many apps, such as editors, tools and CAD, that is actually a plus: every user gets the same interface.
cards.deep: For porting large WPF apps there is the commercial Avalonia XPF. It runs almost unchanged WPF code on macOS and Linux.

cards.q: How does MAUI differ from Avalonia?
options: MAUI turns elements into the system's native controls, Avalonia draws them itself
cards.explain: Hence the trade-off: MAUI looks native, Avalonia looks the same everywhere.

lessons.title: Your first project
lessons.sub: The template, the files and the path to the first window

cards.title: Two commands
cards.body: You install the templates once, then create a project with a single command.
cards.code:
dotnet new install Avalonia.Templates
dotnet new avalonia.mvvm -o MyApp
cd MyApp
dotnet run

cards.title: What is inside
cards.body:
Program.cs: the entry point, sets up Avalonia.
App.axaml: the application and its theme.
App.axaml.cs: creates the main window.
Views/MainWindow.axaml: the window markup.
ViewModels/MainWindowViewModel.cs: the window's data and logic.

The .axaml extension is XAML for Avalonia. It was chosen so IDEs do not confuse it with WPF.

cards.title: Program.cs
cards.body: UsePlatformDetect works out how to open windows on the current system.
cards.code:
public static void Main(string[] args) =>
    BuildAvaloniaApp().StartWithClassicDesktopLifetime(args);

public static AppBuilder BuildAvaloniaApp() =>
    AppBuilder.Configure<App>()
        .UsePlatformDetect()
        .WithInterFont()
        .LogToTrace();

cards.title: App.axaml.cs
cards.body: Once the framework is ready, the app creates the main window and hands it a view model.

cards.q: Put the startup steps in order
cards.explain: Five steps from Main to a window, and you can see each of them in the template code.

cards.q: Match each file to its role
Create a project from the MVVM template
cards.explain: dotnet new creates a project from a template.

cards.q: Why do markup files use .axaml instead of .xaml?
options: So IDEs and tools do not mistake them for WPF markup
cards.explain: Inside, it is XAML with Avalonia's own namespace.

cards.q: Where does the window get its view model?
options: Avalonia finds it by name on its own
cards.explain: DataContext is the key word of the next units: bindings get their data from it.

lessons.title: AXAML: the markup
lessons.sub: Tags are objects, attributes are properties

cards.title: Markup creates objects
cards.body: Each tag is an object, each attribute is one of its properties, and a nested tag is its content.
cards.code:
<Window xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
        xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
        x:Class="MyApp.Views.MainWindow"
        Title="Hello" Width="400" Height="200">
  <Button Content="Click me" HorizontalAlignment="Center"/>
</Window>

cards.title: The same thing in C#
cards.body: Markup is just a convenient notation. You can write the same thing in code:

cards.q: What does the tag <Button Content="Click me"/> do?
options: Creates a Button object and sets its Content property to "Click me"
Calls a method named Click me
cards.explain: Attribute = object property.

cards.q: Which line links the markup to a C# class?
cards.explain: x:Class says: this markup is the other half of the partial class MainWindow.

cards.title: x:Name and code-behind
cards.body: Give an element a name, and C# gets a field with that name. Markup is compiled at build time, so a typo in the name is a compile error, not a crash at run time.

cards.q: A window with a centered button
cards.explain: Avalonia has no Middle. The center is called Center.

cards.q: Match each markup piece to what it means
pairs: A field you can use from code

cards.q: What is true about AXAML? Select all that apply.
options: It is compiled at build time
Any markup can be rewritten as C# code
It runs as a script in the browser
cards.explain: XAML turns into ordinary code at compile time.

cards.q: A Window has a single Content property. How do you put several elements in a window?
options: Put a panel (StackPanel, Grid...) in the window, and the elements in the panel
cards.explain: Panels lay out their children. That is the next unit.

lessons.title: Final: getting started
lessons.sub: Avalonia, the project and the markup

cards.q: What sets Avalonia apart among .NET UI frameworks?
options: It is cross-platform because it does its own rendering
It runs only in the browser
It uses WinForms under the hood
cards.explain: Skia draws everything. The platform only provides a window.

cards.q: From command to window
cards.explain: The template sets up everything you need for a first window.

cards.q: Where is the mistake?
cards.explain: A Window has a single piece of content. The second button is one too many: you need a panel.

cards.q: A name you can use from code
cards.explain: The code-behind gets a SearchBox field.

cards.q: Match each term to its role
pairs: Where the markup gets its data

cards.q: What is true? Select all that apply.
options: Much of your WPF experience carries over
Markup is compiled at build time
cards.explain: Avalonia itself is MIT-licensed. Only the separate XPF product is paid.

cards.q: How does an Avalonia button on a Mac differ from a MAUI button on a Mac?
options: Avalonia draws its button itself, while the MAUI button is a real macOS button
cards.explain: Custom rendering versus native controls.

cards.q: What will the window show?
options: The text "Hello!", with "Demo" in the window title
cards.explain: Title is the window title. TextBlock is the text inside.

units.title: Layout
units.blurb: Measure and Arrange, Margin and Padding, the StackPanel, WrapPanel and DockPanel panels, and Grid with Auto, pixels and stars.

lessons.title: How elements take up space
lessons.sub: Measure and Arrange, alignment, Margin and Padding

cards.title: Two passes
cards.body:
Before drawing, Avalonia asks every element: "How much space do you need?" That is Measure. Then the parent decides and says: "Here is your rectangle." That is Arrange.

A button needs room for its text. How much it actually gets is up to the panel it sits in.

cards.q: Put the layout steps in order
items: The parent asks its children how much they need (Measure)
The children answer with their desired size
The parent gives each one a rectangle (Arrange)
cards.explain: Requests go up, space is handed down.

cards.title: Alignment
cards.body: If the rectangle is bigger than the element needs, alignment decides: HorizontalAlignment = Left, Center, Right or Stretch (fill the space). Most elements default to Stretch.

cards.task: Right now the children sit in a row. Make each one stretch across the full window width, one below another.

cards.title: Margin and Padding
cards.body:
Margin is space outside: from the element to its neighbors.
Padding is space inside: from the border to the content.

Syntax: "10" means all sides, "10,5" means horizontal and vertical, "10,5,10,0" means left, top, right, bottom.

cards.q: The buttons are stuck together. What do you add to each one to get a gap?
cards.explain: Padding would push the text inside the button apart, not the buttons themselves.

cards.q: What does Margin="10,5" mean?
options: 10 left and right, 5 top and bottom
cards.explain: Two numbers mean horizontal and vertical.

cards.q: A centered button with 12 of space around it
cards.explain: Margin is outside, Padding is inside.

cards.q: Match each term to its meaning

lessons.title: Panels
lessons.sub: StackPanel, WrapPanel, DockPanel: how each one lays out

cards.title: The panel decides who goes where
cards.body:
StackPanel: one after another, top to bottom or left to right.
WrapPanel: in a row, and whatever does not fit moves to the next line, like words in text.
DockPanel: docks children to the edges, and the last one fills the rest.
Grid: rows and columns. That is the next lesson.

cards.task: Build a classic window: header at the top, menu on the left, status at the bottom, content takes the rest.

cards.q: Why does the menu in a DockPanel reach all the way down, while the status bar only sits to its right?
options: The menu is docked before the status bar: DockPanel hands out space in child order
The designer drew it that way
cards.explain: Swap the children in the markup, and the status bar spans the whole bottom while the menu gets shorter.

cards.task: The window is narrow, 220 px. Make the items wrap to a new line when they do not fit.

cards.q: What does a horizontal StackPanel do when its children do not fit the width?
options: Nothing: they run off the edge of the window
Wraps them to a new line
cards.explain: Wrapping is WrapPanel's job. StackPanel gives children as much as they ask for in its direction.

cards.task: A toolbar: everything in one row, left to right, at full height.

cards.q: Dock the menu to the left edge
cards.explain: The content comes last, so it fills the rest.

cards.q: Match each panel to its behavior
pairs: To the edges, last one fills the rest

cards.q: What is true? Select all that apply.
options: Child order matters in a DockPanel
The last child of a DockPanel fills the rest
StackPanel wraps items to a new line
WrapPanel wraps items to a new line
cards.explain: The last child fills the rest unless LastChildFill is turned off.

cards.title: Rows and columns
cards.body:
Grid splits space into rows and columns. There are three ways to set a column's width:

200: exactly 200 pixels.
Auto: as much as the content needs.
*: a share of the remaining space. 2* gets twice as much as *.
cards.code:
<Grid ColumnDefinitions="Auto,*,2*" RowDefinitions="Auto,*">
  <TextBlock Grid.Row="0" Grid.Column="0" Text="Icons"/>
  <ListBox   Grid.Row="1" Grid.Column="1"/>
</Grid>

cards.task: The menu on the left is always 200 px, and the content takes everything else. Check it at both window widths.

cards.q: The window is 800 px, columns are "200,*". How much does the second column get?
cards.explain: The star takes whatever is left after fixed and Auto columns: 800 − 200.

cards.task: The icon column fits its content exactly (48 px), and the list is twice as wide as the properties panel.

cards.q: Columns "*,2*,*" in an 800 px window. What are the widths?
cards.explain: There are 4 shares in total, so one share is 200 px.

cards.title: The short syntax is an Avalonia perk
cards.body:
In WPF, columns take a lot of typing: one ColumnDefinition tag each. In Avalonia you can use a string: ColumnDefinitions="Auto,*,2*".

You place an element in a cell with Grid.Row and Grid.Column (counting from zero), and span several with Grid.ColumnSpan.

cards.q: A button in the second column of the first row
cards.explain: Counting starts at zero: the second column is Column="1".

cards.q: What happens to an Auto column if its content gets wider?
options: The column grows, and the star columns get narrower
cards.explain: Auto adapts to its content; stars share what is left.

cards.q: Match each value to its meaning
What is true? Select all that apply.
options: ColumnDefinitions can be set with a string
Stars share the space left after fixed and Auto columns
cards.explain: Auto fits the content. It is not a fixed number.

cards.task: An editor: a 200 px tree on the left, a 100 px panel on the right, and the preview in the middle takes the rest.
Build the window to match the sample.

cards.q: Photo tiles should fill a row and wrap to the next one. Which panel?
cards.explain: Wrapping into rows is what WrapPanel does.

cards.q: Columns are "Auto,*". The first column's content is 120 px, the window is 500 px. What are the widths?
cards.explain: Auto takes 120, the star takes the rest.

cards.q: Which line makes the status bar sit to the right of the menu instead of spanning the full width at the bottom?
cards.code:
<DockPanel>
  <Border DockPanel.Dock="Top"> Header </Border>
  <Border DockPanel.Dock="Left"> Menu </Border>
  <Border DockPanel.Dock="Bottom"> Status </Border>
  <Border> Content </Border>
</DockPanel>
cards.explain: The menu is docked before the status bar, so it took the left strip all the way down. Move the status bar above the menu.

cards.q: Three columns: fit to content, the rest, exactly 150
cards.explain: Columns go from left to right.

cards.q: Match each task to its solution
Who decides how big a button will be?
options: The button says how much it needs, and the parent panel hands out the final rectangle
cards.explain: Measure is a request. Arrange is the parent's decision.

units.title: Bindings and MVVM
units.blurb: DataContext and {Binding}, INotifyPropertyChanged and modes, CommunityToolkit.Mvvm, compiled bindings and commands.

cards.title: Hands off the controls
cards.body:
You could write NameBox.Text = user.Name and then copy it back. But with a dozen fields, the code turns into endless shuffling of values.

A binding links a control's property to a property of a data object. Avalonia moves the values back and forth for you.

cards.title: Where the data comes from
cards.body: Every element has a DataContext: an object with data. If it is not set, the element takes its parent's. Usually you set it on the window, and every element inside sees the same view model.

cards.task: Everything is already set up. Type a name into the TextBox and watch it reach the model and come back in the greeting.

cards.q: The window has DataContext = new MainViewModel(). What is the DataContext of a TextBox inside the window if you do not set it?
options: The same MainViewModel, inherited from the parent
cards.explain: DataContext flows down the tree until someone overrides it.

cards.task: Now change the name from code and check whether the screen updated.

cards.q: Bind the text to the Title property
cards.explain: The binding path is the name of a property on the DataContext.

cards.q: What is true about bindings? Select all that apply.
options: A binding looks up the property on the DataContext
DataContext is inherited from the parent
Bindings spare you from copying values by hand
cards.explain: You can bind any property: numbers, flags, collections, colors.

cards.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: The data object for an element
A link to the Name property
A class holding the window's data

lessons.title: Why the screen did not update

cards.title: The screen does not watch the model on its own
cards.body: A binding does not poll the property every second. The model has to announce it: "my property changed." That is what the INotifyPropertyChanged interface and its PropertyChanged event are for.

cards.task: Code changes the name, but the screen does not budge. Fix the model and check.

cards.q: Why didn't the screen update without INotifyPropertyChanged?
options: The model never raised PropertyChanged, so the binding never learned about the change
cards.explain: No event, no update.

cards.title: Modes
cards.body:
OneWay: from the model to the screen.
TwoWay: both directions (the default for TextBox.Text).
OneTime: once, at startup.
OneWayToSource: only from the screen to the model.

cards.task: Code updates the TextBox, but what the user types never reaches the model. Change the mode.
Pick the mode in which both typing and changes from code show up everywhere.

cards.q: Match each mode to its direction
Which line makes the screen update?
cards.explain: OnPropertyChanged raises the PropertyChanged event with the property name.

cards.q: The user typed some text, the model got it, but the greeting (a TextBlock bound to the same property) did not update. What is wrong?
options: The model did not raise PropertyChanged, so other bindings to Name never heard about the change
cards.explain: That is exactly what the first exercise without INotifyPropertyChanged showed.

cards.title: Model, View, ViewModel
cards.body:
View: the markup, only how things look.
ViewModel: what to show and what to do. Properties and commands, not a single control.
Model: data and business logic.

A ViewModel is easy to test: no windows, just C#.

cards.q: In MVVM, where should the "email is valid" check live?
options: In the ViewModel (or Model), where there are no controls and testing is easy
In a click handler in code-behind
cards.explain: The View only displays. Logic lives in C# classes with no UI.

cards.title: A generator writes the code for you
cards.body: Writing OnPropertyChanged in every property gets old fast. The CommunityToolkit.Mvvm package generates it at build time.

cards.q: A notifying property in one line
cards.explain: The generator creates a Title property.

cards.q: Why is the class marked partial?
options: The generator writes the second half of the class: the properties and notifications
cards.explain: Your half has the fields and logic. The generated half has the properties.

cards.title: Compiled bindings
cards.body:
A regular binding finds the property through reflection at run time: one typo, and the field is just empty. With x:DataType, Avalonia checks bindings at build time and generates fast code.

Avalonia 11 templates turn them on by default.
cards.code:
<Window x:DataType="vm:MainViewModel">
  <TextBox Text="{Binding Nmae}"/>   <!-- build error: no property Nmae -->
</Window>

cards.q: What do compiled bindings give you? Select all that apply.
options: Mistakes in property names show up at build time
They work with Native AOT and trimming
cards.explain: You still need a DataContext. x:DataType just tells the compiler its type.

cards.q: Match each term to its role
pairs: What to show and what to do

cards.q: The Avalonia template offers CommunityToolkit.Mvvm or ReactiveUI. What is the difference?
options: The Toolkit is source generators and simple attributes; ReactiveUI is a reactive approach built on event streams (Rx)
cards.explain: The Toolkit is easier to start with. ReactiveUI shines in complex reactive logic.

cards.title: A button calls a model method
cards.body: In MVVM, a button does not call a handler in code-behind. Its Command property is bound to a command in the ViewModel.

cards.title: In the markup
cards.body: The generated command is named after the method plus "Command".

cards.q: Bind the button to the Delete() method
cards.explain: [RelayCommand] on Delete() creates DeleteCommand.

cards.title: When the button is unavailable
cards.body: A command can say "I can't run right now" through CanExecute. The button grays itself out.

cards.q: Why put [NotifyCanExecuteChangedFor(nameof(SaveCommand))] on the Name property?
options: When Name changes, the button asks CanSave again and enables or disables itself
It will not compile without it
cards.explain: Otherwise the button never learns that the condition changed.

cards.title: Async commands
cards.body: If the method is async Task, the generator creates an AsyncRelayCommand. While it runs, the command has IsRunning = true, and you cannot press it again.

cards.q: What will the command for the LoadAsync() method be called?
options: LoadCommand: the Async suffix is dropped
cards.explain: The generator strips Async from the name.

cards.q: What is true? Select all that apply.
options: A button with a command disables itself when CanExecute = false
An async Task method gives you an AsyncRelayCommand
Commands must be called from code-behind
cards.explain: In MVVM, code-behind is nearly empty.

cards.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Generate a command from a method
The async command is still running

lessons.title: Final: bindings and MVVM
lessons.sub: Data finds its own way to the screen

cards.task: Everything is broken: OneTime mode and a model with no notifications. Make both typing and changes from code show up everywhere.

cards.q: A binding points to the property Nmae (a typo). What happens with compiled bindings?
options: An empty field at run time
cards.explain: Without x:DataType you would get a silently empty field.

cards.q: Why won't the screen update when code changes Count?
cards.explain: A plain auto-property does not raise PropertyChanged. You need [ObservableProperty] private int _count;

cards.q: Wire the "Add" button to the Add() method
cards.explain: Click is an event for code-behind. In MVVM you use Command.

cards.q: What belongs in a ViewModel? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: A ViewModel knows nothing about controls.

cards.q: Match each symptom to its cause
pairs: Code changes a property, the screen stays put
Field is empty with no errors

cards.q: What is the default mode for TextBox.Text?
cards.explain: The whole point of an input field is to send data back to the model.

cards.q: The path of a value as the user types
items: The user types into the TextBox
The TwoWay binding writes the value to Name
Other bindings to Name update the screen
cards.explain: Without step three, there is no step four.

units.title: Styles, lists and the UI thread
units.blurb: Style selectors and pseudo-classes, themes and resources, lists with ObservableCollection and DataTemplate, Dispatcher.UIThread. The course final.

cards.title: The selector picks, the setter changes
cards.body: An Avalonia style looks a lot like a CSS rule: the selector says which elements it applies to, and the setters say what to change.
cards.code:
<Style Selector="Button.primary">
  <Setter Property="Background" Value="#4f7cff"/>
  <Setter Property="Foreground" Value="White"/>
</Style>

<Button Classes="primary" Content="Save"/>

cards.title: Selector basics
cards.body:
Button: by type.
.primary: by class (Classes="primary").
#Save: by name (x:Name="Save").
StackPanel Button: a button anywhere inside a StackPanel.
StackPanel > Button: direct children only.

cards.task: Select every button in the window.
Only the buttons sitting directly in the toolbar (not inside the Border).
All buttons inside the toolbar, at any depth.
Only the heading.

cards.title: Pseudo-classes
cards.body: Element states use a colon: :pointerover (the mouse is over the element), :pressed, :disabled, :focus.
cards.deep: Why /template/ ContentPresenter? The Fluent theme paints the hover background on an inner element of the button's template. A style on the button itself loses, so you need to target the same part of the template.

cards.q: How does "StackPanel Button" differ from "StackPanel > Button"?
options: The first matches buttons at any depth inside, the second only direct children
cards.explain: Just like CSS: a space means descendant, > means child.

cards.q: Match each selector to what it selects
Which selectors match <Button Classes="primary danger"/>? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Several classes in a row means the element must have all of them. The button has no warning class.

cards.q: Give the button the Button.danger style
cards.explain: The Classes property is a space-separated list of classes.

lessons.title: Themes and resources
lessons.sub: Fluent, light and dark, StaticResource and DynamicResource

cards.title: A theme is a set of styles for every control
cards.body:
App.axaml includes a theme, such as FluentTheme. It defines how every standard control looks.

A theme comes in variants: light and dark.

cards.q: RequestedThemeVariant="Default". Which theme will you get?
options: Whatever the system uses: light or dark
cards.explain: Light or Dark must be set explicitly.

cards.title: Resources: define a color once
cards.body: Colors, brushes and sizes go into resources under a key, and you use them by key. Change it in one place, and it changes everywhere.

cards.title: Static or Dynamic
cards.body:
StaticResource looks up the resource once, at load time.
DynamicResource keeps watching it: if the resource changes (say, the theme switches), the element updates.

For theme-dependent colors, use DynamicResource.

cards.q: The user switched to the dark theme, but one button stayed light. What is the likely cause?
options: Its color comes from StaticResource, which does not track changes
The dark theme does not support buttons
cards.explain: DynamicResource would have updated along with the theme.

cards.title: A separate color for each theme
cards.body: You can define a resource separately for the light and dark themes with ThemeDictionaries.
cards.code:
<ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries>
  <ResourceDictionary x:Key="Light">
    <SolidColorBrush x:Key="Panel" Color="#f3f3f3"/>
  </ResourceDictionary>
  <ResourceDictionary x:Key="Dark">
    <SolidColorBrush x:Key="Panel" Color="#1e1e1e"/>
  </ResourceDictionary>
</ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries>

cards.q: A background that changes along with the theme
cards.explain: StaticResource would grab the color only once.

cards.q: Match each term to what it does
pairs: Light, dark or follow the system

cards.q: What is true? Select all that apply.
options: A theme defines the look of every standard control
ThemeDictionaries set different values for Light and Dark
DynamicResource updates when the theme changes
A resource can be used in only one place
cards.explain: The whole point of a resource is to use it everywhere.

cards.title: A list from a collection
cards.body: A ListBox shows a collection from the ViewModel. A DataTemplate describes how a single item looks.
cards.code:
<ListBox ItemsSource="{Binding People}">
  <ListBox.ItemTemplate>
    <DataTemplate x:DataType="m:Person">
      <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Spacing="8">
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding Name}"/>
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding Age}"/>
      </StackPanel>
    </DataTemplate>
  </ListBox.ItemTemplate>
</ListBox>

cards.q: Inside a DataTemplate, where does {Binding Name} look for Name?
options: On the current list item, the Person object
cards.explain: Each row's DataContext is its own item from the collection.

cards.title: Added it, but the list did not change
cards.body: A plain List<T> does not announce that an item was added. ObservableCollection<T> does, through the CollectionChanged event, and the ListBox shows the new row right away.

cards.q: People is a List<Person>. A command adds a person, but the list on screen does not change. Why?
options: List<T> does not announce changes; you need ObservableCollection<T>
cards.explain: Same idea as PropertyChanged, but for collections.

cards.title: Thousands of rows
cards.body: ListBox virtualizes by default: it creates controls only for visible rows and reuses them as you scroll. That is why a list of 100,000 items stays smooth.
cards.deep: Virtualization breaks if you put a ListBox inside a StackPanel: the panel gives its child infinite height, so the ListBox creates controls for every row. Give the list a bounded height, such as a star row in a Grid.

cards.q: Show the Orders collection
cards.explain: In Avalonia 11 it is ItemsSource. Items remains for items added directly in markup.

cards.q: Which line makes a 100,000-row list slow?
cards.explain: StackPanel gives the list infinite height, which turns virtualization off. Use a Grid with RowDefinitions="Auto,*".

cards.q: Match each term to its meaning
What is true? Select all that apply.
options: A row's DataContext is an item from the collection
ObservableCollection updates the ListBox on Add and Remove
Changing a property inside Person also needs PropertyChanged on Person
List<T> updates the ListBox on its own
cards.explain: ObservableCollection tracks which items are in it, not the properties of those items.

cards.title: One thread for the UI
cards.body: As in WPF and Unity, Avalonia controls can be touched only from the UI thread. From any other thread you get InvalidOperationException: Call from invalid thread.

cards.q: A background thread writes to TextBlock.Text. What happens?
options: The text updates after a delay
cards.explain: Controls check which thread is accessing them.

cards.title: Ask the UI thread
cards.body: Dispatcher.UIThread is the UI thread's queue.

cards.title: Most of the time you do not need Dispatcher
cards.body: In an async command, await brings you back to the UI thread on its own: Avalonia installs its own SynchronizationContext. Hand heavy computation to Task.Run and assign the result after await.

cards.q: A command computes for 3 seconds right on the UI thread, and the window freezes. How do you fix it?
options: Move the computation to Task.Run and await it
cards.explain: Post also runs the computation on the UI thread, so the window still freezes.

cards.q: Update the status from a background thread
cards.explain: Post queues the action on the UI thread.

cards.q: Which line will crash?
cards.explain: System.Timers.Timer calls its handler on the thread pool. You need Dispatcher.UIThread.Post or a DispatcherTimer.
